title: ProcMEM: Learning Reusable Procedural Memory from Experience via Non-Parametric PPO for LLM Agents
claim: Retrieving past experience forces costly reasoning at decision time; encoding it as executable procedures maps situations directly to actions.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, metaphor illustrations with a bottom caption flow under each
description: Two side-by-side illustrated panels split by a thin vertical line. The left panel is titled 'Episodic Memory as History Book'. It shows a large, worn, brown open book labeled 'Past Trajectories / Interaction History'. A stressed robot with its hands on its head stands in front of it. Above the book are a magnifying glass over text, linked photo-like scenes, and a tangle of arrows with question marks. The caption reads 'Retrieve → Interpret → Reason → Action (High Cognitive Cost)'. The right panel is titled 'Procedural Memory as Executable Script' and uses a clean cyan, glowing style. It shows stacked folder cards with a highlighted code-like box ('PROCEDURE: TASK_DECOMPOSITION, EXECUTE, MAP_ACTION') and an arrow pointing right. A calm robot points at a puzzle-piece skill icon. A small 'Situation → Action' box sits below. The caption reads 'Situation → Executable Strategy (Low Cognitive Cost)'. Contrast between messy sepia and clean cyan draws the eye first.
caption: Episodic memory versus procedural memory in LLM-driven agents. Episodic memory retrieves past interactions for reference, requiring inference-heavy reasoning at decision time. Procedural memory encodes reusable procedural Skills that directly map situations to actions, enabling efficient experience reuse.
abstract: LLM-driven agents demonstrate strong performance in sequential decision-making but often rely on on-the-fly reasoning, re-deriving solutions even in recurring scenarios. This insufficient experience reuse leads to computational redundancy and execution instability. To bridge this gap, we propose ProcMEM, a framework that enables agents to autonomously learn procedural memory from interaction experiences without parameter updates. By formalizing a Skill-MDP, ProcMEM transforms passive episodic narratives into executable Skills defined by activation, execution, and termination conditions to ensure executability. To achieve reliable reusability without capability degradation, we introduce Non-Parametric PPO, which leverages semantic gradients for high-quality candidate generation and a PPO Gate for robust Skill verification. Through score-based maintenance, ProcMEM sustains compact, high-quality procedural memory. Experimental results across in-domain, cross-task, and cross-agent scenarios demonstrate that ProcMEM achieves \textbf{superior reuse rates and significant performance gains} with extreme memory compression. Visualized evolutionary trajectories and Skill distributions further reveal how ProcMEM transparently accumulates, refines, and reuses procedural knowledge to facilitate long-term autonomy.
